scenes.visual: Title card 'Emptying Islands' over a cartoon of a tiny red mangrove island standing on prop roots in shallow, clear water. Reuse the first film's colour map: BLUE = immigration of new species, RED = local extinction, GOLD = S*. Species tokens for the three mites: GREEN = present before and after (Bdella), GREY = present before only (Amblyseius), PURPLE = present after only (Carpoglyphus). Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Islands, tents and animals are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; the richness-over-time plot is labelled 'schematic, shape only'.

scenes.tts: The worked island refilled on paper, toward a steady count, while species kept coming and going. So empty a real island of every insect and spider. How many species come back, and are they the same ones?
scenes.visual: A small inset recaps the first film's graph: BLUE and RED lines crossing at the GOLD dot. It shrinks to a corner badge. A mangrove island appears full of small cartoon insects and spiders; they fade out, leaving it empty, and two question marks appear: 'how many?' and 'which ones?'.
scenes.narration: The worked island refilled on paper, toward a steady count, while species kept coming and going. So empty a real island of every insect and spider. How many species come back, and are they the same ones?

scenes.tts: Most islands were colonised long ago, so nobody saw their rates from the start. Daniel Simberloff and Edward Wilson chose islands small enough to empty, and then watched them fill.
scenes.visual: An old, full island with a faded label 'colonised long ago: rates unseen'. Then name cards 'Daniel Simberloff' and 'Edward O. Wilson' slide in beside a map of the Florida Keys, where six small dots light up.
scenes.narration: Most islands were colonised long ago, so nobody saw their rates from the start. Daniel Simberloff and Edward Wilson chose islands small enough to empty, and then watched them fill.

scenes.tts: They used six small islands of red mangrove in the Florida Keys. Each carried a community of terrestrial arthropods: insects, spiders, mites and their relatives.
scenes.visual: Zoom to one of the six dots: a small red mangrove island on arching prop roots. Labels: 'red mangrove, Rhizophora mangle' and 'six small islands'. Cartoon beetle, spider, mite and moth appear on the leaves with the label 'terrestrial arthropods'.
scenes.narration: They used six small islands of red mangrove in the Florida Keys. Each carried a community of terrestrial arthropods: insects, spiders, mites and their relatives.

scenes.tts: First they recorded every arthropod species on each island. Then they covered each island with a tent and fumigated it. Afterwards they censused the islands again and again for a year.
scenes.visual: Three steps, each with a numbered tag. 1: an open notebook fills with coloured species tokens, 'census before'. 2: a tent drops over the whole island and a pale cloud fills it, 'tent and fumigation'. 3: the tent lifts on an empty island and a calendar strip runs from day 0 to day 365 with tick marks for repeated censuses.
scenes.narration: First they recorded every arthropod species on each island. Then they covered each island with a tent and fumigated it. Afterwards they censused the islands again and again for a year.

scenes.tts: The count climbed back. By about day two hundred and fifty, most islands held about as many species as untreated islands. The exception was E one, the most distant. Population densities, though, were still abnormally low.
scenes.caption: The count climbed back. By about day 250, most islands held about as many species as untreated islands. The exception was E1, the most distant. Population densities, though, were still abnormally low.
scenes.visual: A plot of species number against days since fumigation. A shaded band marks 'untreated islands'. Five rising curves reach the band near day 250 (marked on screen); a sixth, labelled 'E1, most distant', stays below it. Schematic, shape only. Then the leaves show only a few animals of each kind: 'densities still low'.
scenes.narration: The count climbed back. By about day 250, most islands held about as many species as untreated islands. The exception was E1, the most distant. Population densities, though, were still abnormally low.

scenes.tts: Now the second question. The count came back. How much of the old species list do you expect the new list to share?
scenes.visual: Two notebooks side by side: 'before' and 'day 364', each with the same number of tokens but the colours hidden under grey covers. A question mark sits between them.
scenes.narration: Now the second question. The count came back. How much of the old species list do you expect the new list to share?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two covered notebooks; a 5-second timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: Take three mite kinds from island E nine, chosen because their records are clear. One was there before and after. One was there only before. One was there only after.
scenes.caption: Take three mite kinds from island E9, chosen because their records are clear. One was there before and after. One was there only before. One was there only after.
scenes.visual: The covers lift on three cartoon mites only. GREEN 'Bdella' appears in both notebooks. GREY 'Amblyseius' appears only in 'before'. PURPLE 'Carpoglyphus lactis' appears only in 'day 364'. Label 'island E9, three chosen mite taxa'. The names stay on screen; they are not spoken.
scenes.narration: Take three mite kinds from island E9, chosen because their records are clear. One was there before and after. One was there only before. One was there only after.

scenes.tts: Two kinds before, and two kinds after, so the count is unchanged. But only one of the three is shared. The Jaccard similarity is shared species divided by species in either list. Here it is one in three.
scenes.caption: Two kinds before, and two kinds after, so the count is unchanged. But only one of the three is shared. The Jaccard similarity is shared species divided by species in either list. Here it is 1/3.
scenes.visual: Counters '2' and '2' over the notebooks with an equals sign. A Venn diagram forms: GREY in the left circle only, GREEN in the overlap, PURPLE in the right circle only. On screen: 'Jaccard = shared / in either list = 1/3'.
scenes.narration: Two kinds before, and two kinds after, so the count is unchanged. But only one of the three is shared. The Jaccard similarity is shared species divided by species in either list. Here it is 1/3.

scenes.tts: Read it with care. These three are a chosen subset, not the whole community. And finding the shared mite at both censuses does not mean it survived. It was recorded again after recolonisation.
scenes.caption: Read it with care. These three are a chosen subset, not the whole community. And finding the shared mite at both censuses does not mean it survived. It was recorded again after recolonisation.
scenes.visual: The three mites shrink into a small highlighted corner of a much larger notebook page full of other tokens, labelled 'a selection, not the whole community'. The GREEN Bdella token fades out at the tent, then fades back in later on the calendar strip: 'recorded again, not necessarily survived'.
scenes.narration: Read it with care. These three are a chosen subset, not the whole community. And finding the shared mite at both censuses does not mean it survived. It was recorded again after recolonisation.

scenes.tts: A second report followed four islands to the end of the second year. Species numbers had changed little from the year before, while immigrations and extinctions continued at high rates.
scenes.visual: The richness plot extends to a second year, shown as sparse census points, not continuous curves: for each of four islands, a year-one census point and a year-two census point joined by a dashed, near-horizontal line labelled 'little net change between annual censuses; path between them unknown'. Above them, BLUE arrows (arrivals) and RED arrows (losses) keep firing into and out of the island at irregular intervals, labelled 'immigrations and extinctions continued at high rates'.
scenes.narration: A second report followed four islands to the end of the second year. Species numbers had changed little from the year before, while immigrations and extinctions continued at high rates.

scenes.tts: A steady count with continuing replacement is what the model calls a dynamic equilibrium. The result fits the model, though on its own it does not prove the model's mechanism.
scenes.visual: The corner badge of the first film's graph grows back: the GOLD dot pulses with BLUE and RED arrows cycling through it. Label 'dynamic equilibrium'. A small stamp reads 'fits the model, does not prove it'.
scenes.narration: A steady count with continuing replacement is what the model calls a dynamic equilibrium. The result fits the model, though on its own it does not prove the model's mechanism.

scenes.tts: And the rates themselves were rough. Censuses came at intervals, so some arrivals and losses fell between visits and were never seen. And a resident overlooked at one census looked like a loss and a return.
scenes.visual: The calendar strip with census ticks. Between two ticks, a PURPLE token flies in and blinks out unseen, shown in dashed outline: 'missed between visits'. Then a GREEN token is hidden behind a leaf at one census tick and visible at the next, labelled 'overlooked: looks like a loss and a return'.
scenes.narration: And the rates themselves were rough. Censuses came at intervals, so some arrivals and losses fell between visits and were never seen. And a resident overlooked at one census looked like a loss and a return.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'A steady species count can hide a changing list of species.'
